section.title: Concern for the Corinthians
section.sectionRationale: The fool's speech ends and the pastor's heart is laid bare. Paul insists he is in no way inferior to the super-apostles, for the marks of a true apostle were done among the Corinthians, yet he calls himself nothing. He will not be a burden; he seeks not their possessions but them, spending and being spent for their souls like a parent for children. The section closes with his fear that when he comes he will find quarreling, jealousy, and unrepented sin.
section.thesis: A true apostle is marked not by self-promotion but by self-giving love that seeks the people rather than their possessions, and by a holy jealousy for their repentance and growth in Christ.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the marks of a true apostle done among them; the parent who spends and is spent for the children's souls; and the pastor's fear of finding sin and disorder when he comes.

units.label: The marks of a true apostle
units.note: in no way inferior, yet nothing

verses.text: I have become a fool, but you drove me to it. In fact, you should have commended me, since I am in no way inferior to those “super-apostles,” even though I am nothing.
The marks of a true apostle, {{semeion|signs}}, wonders, and miracles, were performed among you with great perseverance.
In what way were you inferior to the other churches, except that I was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong!

units.label: I will spend and be spent

verses.text: See, I am ready to come to you a third time, and I will not be a burden, because I am not seeking your possessions, but you. For children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.
And for the sake of your souls, I will most gladly spend my money and myself. If I {{agapao|love}} you more, will you love me less?
Be that as it may, I was not a burden to you; but crafty as I am, I caught you by trickery.
Did I exploit you by anyone I sent you?
I urged Titus to visit you, and I sent our brother with him. Did Titus exploit you in any way? Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps?

units.label: Fear of finding sin
units.note: to build you up, not tear you down

verses.text: Have you been thinking all along that we were making a defense to you? We speak before God in Christ, and all of this, beloved, is to {{oikodome|build you up}}.

For I am afraid that when I come, I may not find you as I wish, and you may not find me as you wish. I fear that there may be quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, and disorder.

I am afraid that when I come again, my God will humble me before you, and I will be grieved over many who have sinned earlier and have not repented of their acts of impurity, sexual immorality, and debauchery.

semeion.gloss: A sign, a token that points beyond itself to a deeper reality. Paul lists signs, wonders, and miracles as the marks of a true apostle worked among the Corinthians. A sign is never an end in itself; it authenticates the messenger and points to the God who sends him. Paul notes these were done with great perseverance, so that his very endurance was itself part of the credential.

agapao.gloss: To love with self-giving, sacrificial love, the love that seeks the good of the other regardless of return. Paul loves the Corinthians this way, gladly spending his money and himself for their souls even if they love him less. This is the love of a parent for a child, and ultimately the love of God in Christ, who gave Himself for those who could give nothing back.

oikodome.gloss: Building up, edification, the strengthening and growth of a person or community as a house is raised. Paul insists that everything he writes, even his sharp words, is aimed not at self-defense but at building up the Corinthians. The image runs through the letter: the authority Christ gave the apostle is for construction, not demolition, for the maturing of the church in the faith.

basic.context: Paul finishes the reluctant boasting and speaks plainly as their spiritual father. He says he is in no way behind the so-called super-apostles, for the true marks of an apostle, signs and wonders and patient endurance, were seen among them, yet he calls himself nothing. He refuses to be a financial burden, insisting he wants them and not their money, and he will gladly spend himself for their souls. Then he opens his heart about his fear: that when he comes he will find quarreling, jealousy, and people who have not repented of serious sin.
basic.hermeneutics: This section shifts from irony to earnest love. Read the boasting of chapters 11 and 12 as forced by the false teachers, and this passage as the reason behind it: Paul cares for these people. His refusal of support, his parent language, and his fear of finding sin all reveal what a true minister looks like. Verse 19 gives the key: all of this is to build them up, not to defend himself.
basic.originalLanguages: The marks of an apostle include semeion, signs, tokens that point beyond themselves to God. Paul's care is agapao, self-giving love that spends itself for the beloved. And the whole aim, even of his sharp words, is oikodome, building up, the raising of the church like a house rather than its tearing down.
basic.typology: Paul's model of a parent who spends and is spent for the children reflects the fatherhood of God and supremely the Son who gave Himself. As the prophets grieved over Israel's unrepentant sin, so Paul grieves over Corinth, standing in the line of shepherds who long for their people to return. His refusal to exploit contrasts with the hirelings and false shepherds of Scripture.
basic.christ: The self-spending love Paul shows is the love of Christ flowing through His servant, the One who did not seek what was ours but us, and who gave Himself for our souls. Paul speaks before God in Christ and works for the building up of Christ's body. His holy grief over sin mirrors the Lord who wept over an unrepentant city and calls His people to repentance and holiness.
basic.god: It is God whom Paul serves and before whom he speaks, and God who may humble him by the state he finds at Corinth. This is a God who cares about the moral life of His church, grieved by impurity and disorder, and who works through faithful ministers to build His people up. He is the God of a love that gives rather than grasps.
basic.crossReferences: John 10 contrasts the good shepherd who lays down his life with the hireling. 1 Thessalonians 2 shows Paul as a nursing mother and a father with his children. Romans 15 speaks of building up the neighbor rather than pleasing oneself.
basic.oneStory: Throughout Scripture God gives shepherds to His people and grieves when they exploit the flock, promising at last a Shepherd who gives Himself. Paul embodies that self-giving love, seeking the people and not their goods, spending himself for their souls. The story runs toward Christ, whose love builds up His church and calls her from sin into holiness.

context.literary:
This passage closes the fool's speech and opens the way to the last chapter of the letter. It falls into three parts. Verses 11 to 13 pick up the boast and put an end to it: Paul says the Corinthians drove him to it and ought to have commended him. Verses 14 to 18 turn on the idea of burden, with the word returning in verses 13, 14 and 16, and move through a series of questions about money and trust. Verses 19 to 21 step back and say what the whole speech was for and what he fears.

The rhetoric changes in the middle. The first section is still ironic: 'Forgive me this wrong!' in verse 13 is mock apology, and 'crafty as I am, I caught you by trickery' in verse 16 repeats a charge from his critics in a voice of heavy sarcasm. Then the sarcasm drops away and the tone softens into the language of a family. The parent who saves for the children in verse 14, and the parent who gladly spends and is spent in verse 15, are not images of a debater. They are the speech of someone who loves.

The questions in verses 15 to 18 are a rapid cross examination of the Corinthians' own memory. 'Did I exploit you by anyone I sent you?' The expected answer is no, and the reader is invited to supply it. The reference to Titus connects this passage to the earlier parts of the letter, where Titus was sent to Corinth and brought back good news, 7:6 to 7 and 8:16 to 17.

Verse 19 is the hinge of the whole fool's speech. The Corinthians have been thinking that Paul has been defending himself to them, but he says he speaks 'before God in Christ,' and that everything is to build them up. The speech that looked like self defence is in fact pastoral care. The final verses 20 and 21 supply a catalogue of vices in two lists, one of eight social sins and one of three sexual ones, and the two fears that frame them: that he will not find them as he wishes and they will not find him as they wish, and that God will humble him before them. These lead straight into the warnings of chapter 13.
context.historical:
The 'third time' of verse 14 refers to a pattern of visits that can be pieced together from the letters. The first was the founding visit of about a year and a half, Acts 18:1 to 11. The second, between the two letters, was painful, which 2:1 hints at and 13:2 confirms when Paul says he had already warned them 'the second time I was with you.' The third is the visit he is now preparing to make, and he states in 13:1 that this is the third time he is coming.

The question of support was a sensitive point in a patronage society. Paul had a right to be paid by the churches, as he argues in 1 Corinthians 9, but he supported himself by his trade, Acts 18:3, and accepted gifts from other churches when he was in need. In Corinth this was apparently used against him. Verse 16 shows the form of the charge: that he had not taken money openly but had found a trick to gain from them through others, perhaps through the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, which was being organised at the time, chapters 8 and 9. Paul answers by pointing to Titus and the brother who went with him, and asks whether they took advantage of anyone. The collection, administered by named and trusted representatives, was handled in the open, 8:20 to 21.

The 'marks of an apostle' in verse 12 are 'signs, wonders and miracles.' Paul does not elaborate. In Romans 15:18 and 19 he speaks of Christ working through him 'by the power of signs and wonders, and by the power of the Spirit of God,' and Hebrews 2:4 links the same terms with God's confirmation of the message. In Corinth, where miraculous gifts were widely valued, Paul's claim was probably not disputed. His point is that his authority did not depend on any more display than the church had already seen.

The vices of verse 20 sound like a description of a divided, status minded congregation. 1 Corinthians 3:3 had already named jealousy and dissension among them. The sexual sins of verse 21 fit a city whose name had become shorthand for loose living, and 1 Corinthians 5 and 6 had already dealt with them.
context.canonical:
The picture of a leader who spends himself for those he serves has an Old Testament background in the shepherd who cares for the flock. Ezekiel 34 condemns the shepherds who feed themselves and do not feed the sheep, and promises that God Himself will search for His flock. Paul stands with the true shepherds and against the false: he is not seeking their possessions but them.

The language of the parent and child appears across Paul's letters. In 1 Corinthians 4:15 he says that in Christ Jesus he became their father through the gospel. In 1 Thessalonians 2:7 and 8 he writes that he was gentle among them like a nursing mother, so deeply caring that he was delighted to share not only the gospel but his own life as well, and in verse 9 that he worked night and day so as not to burden anyone. In Acts 20:33 to 35 he reminds the Ephesian elders that he coveted no one's silver or gold, and quotes the Lord Jesus: 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.' In Philippians 2:17 he is glad to be poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of their faith.

The vices of verse 20 belong to a standard biblical list. Galatians 5:19 to 21 gives a closely similar list of the works of the flesh, including strife, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish ambition, dissension and factions. Romans 1:29 to 31 and 1 Corinthians 3:3 run along the same lines. The call to repent of sexual sin in verse 21 echoes 1 Corinthians 6:9 to 11 and Galatians 5:19.

The principle of verse 19, that everything is to build up the church, is repeated in Romans 14:19, 1 Corinthians 14:26 and Ephesians 4:12 to 16. The warning of verse 21 has an Old Testament pattern in the prophets' grief over unrepentant Israel, and finds a New Testament echo in Jesus weeping over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul intended the Corinthians to hear a change of voice. The ironic debater of the fool's speech gives way to a father, and he wants them to recognise the difference. He has no need for their approval, and he says plainly that he is not defending himself, but he is not indifferent to what happens to them either. The heart of the passage is a statement of motive: 'I am not seeking your possessions, but you.'

He also meant to take the weapon of money out of the hands of his critics. Whether or not his accusers were right that he had never taken a penny, he does not argue the point; he simply asks them to look at the people he sent, and he lets the record of Titus speak.

Finally, he meant to prepare them for his coming. The list of fears in verses 20 and 21 is not a threat but a warning given early, so that they can repent before he arrives. He wants his visit to be a joy and not a judgment. The structure of the passage, ending on grief and repentance, shows that the point of all his rhetoric is the church's holiness.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records Paul's own decision not to burden the Corinthians, and the plans for his next visit. It does not make it a rule that ministers must refuse support, and 1 Corinthians 9:14 says the opposite is the Lord's command for those who preach. What it describes is a particular pastor's way of loving a particular congregation.

The verse about children saving up for parents is a proverb of how families normally work and not a rule about financial duties. Elsewhere Paul teaches that children ought to care for aged parents, 1 Timothy 5:4, so verse 14 is not setting it aside. It says that in the relationship between a founder and a church, the movement of giving runs from the older to the younger.

What does carry forward is the shape of the ministry: love that seeks the people and not what they can give, honesty in handling money, a readiness to spend and be spent, and a willingness to name sin in the church for the sake of its repentance. A congregation can also draw from the passage a standard by which to judge those who lead it, and a reminder that the vices in verse 20 are never harmless in a body that belongs to Christ.

debates.question: Does 2 Corinthians 10 to 13 belong with chapters 1 to 9, or is it a separate letter?

views.label: One letter with a change of tone
views.case: All the manuscripts have the letter as it stands, and the themes of boasting, weakness, money and the collection run through both halves. The change of tone can be explained by a shift of audience, from the repentant majority in chapters 1 to 9 to the resistant minority in chapters 10 to 13, or by news from Corinth arriving between two sittings of writing. Paul's references to the visit and to Titus fit a single storyline.

views.label: Chapters 10 to 13 are part of the earlier painful letter
views.case: Others hold that the sharp tone does not fit the relief of chapter 7, where Paul is glad that the Corinthians have repented, and that chapters 10 to 13 are the 'tearful letter' mentioned in 2:3 and 2:4 or part of it. The present form would then be the work of an editor. The difficulty is that 13:2 and 12:14 look forward to a visit not yet made, while 2:3 says the earlier letter was meant to spare them a visit.

views.label: A letter written after receiving new bad news
views.case: A third view is that chapters 1 to 9 were sent first, and that fresh trouble from the rivals reached Paul afterwards, so he added chapters 10 to 13 in a second letter. The shift in the church's mood explains the change in the writing.

debates.bearing: The passage can be read well on any of these views. In all of them the final chapters show Paul's love as strongly as his anger, and the content of the pastoral teaching, that a true apostle seeks the people and not their possessions, stands the same.

debates.question: What is the point of 'crafty as I am, I caught you by trickery' in verse 16?

views.label: Sarcasm repeating the charge
views.case: The phrase follows a line of rhetorical questions in which Paul answers an accusation, probably that he had enriched himself through his delegates. Paul states the charge in its most absurd form and lets the Corinthians see how far it is from the facts. The words 'as I am' mark a mocking tone, and verses 17 and 18 answer it.

views.label: A real accusation that Paul quotes without endorsing
views.case: Others read the verse as a quotation from the critics that Paul repeats in order to answer. The two readings are close, since both agree that Paul does not accept the charge. The difference is whether the voice is Paul's own irony or the critics' words in his mouth.

debates.bearing: Either way, Paul's reply is to point to his sent men and the record of Titus. The lesson is that a minister's integrity should be open to checking, and that sound financial practice and trustworthy associates are part of the protection of the gospel.

study.originalLanguages:
The question of Paul's apostolic marks begins with three nouns in verse 12: semeia, signs, terata, wonders, and dynameis, miracles or acts of power. The list is the same one that appears in Acts 2:22 of Jesus, in Romans 15:19 of Paul and in Hebrews 2:4 of the apostolic witness. The three words describe one reality from three sides: a pointer to God, an astonishing event, and an expression of His power. The sentence ends with hypomone, 'perseverance,' which stands before the signs in the Greek order and makes patient endurance, and not the miracle, the thing Paul stresses first.

In verse 13 Paul says 'Forgive me this wrong!' using the verb charizomai, to grant as a favour, a gift. It comes from charis, grace, so he is asking them to give him a grace. The irony is complete: the 'wrong' is that he did not ask them for money, and he sets the request in the vocabulary of the gospel.

The word 'burden' is katanarkao in verses 13 and 14, a heavy verb that means to weigh down or to be a dead weight on someone. In verse 14 he says he will not be a burden, 'because I am not seeking your possessions, but you,' with ta hymon and hymas set side by side in the Greek, 'your things, but you.' The contrast is as sharp in Greek as in English. And the proverb that follows uses thesaurizo, to store up as treasure, the verb Jesus uses in Matthew 6:19 to 20.

Verse 15 has Paul say that he will 'gladly spend and be spent,' with two verbs, dapanao and ekdapanao. The second is the first with a prefix that intensifies it, so that the sense is to spend and be utterly spent. The verb is passive, which suggests that he will let himself be used up. It is a stronger expression than the English suggests. The next sentence asks whether, loving more, he is to be loved less, a gentle question that exposes the unfairness of their response.

The verbs in verse 16, 'crafty,' panourgos, and 'trickery,' dolos, belong to the same family as the 'cunning' used of the serpent in 11:3. Paul takes the label and uses it in irony.

In verse 18 the 'footsteps' are ichne, the tracks left by walking, which the BSB footnote says is literally 'in the same footsteps' as a separate question: 'Not in the same footsteps?' The point is that Titus and Paul leave the same marks, and the verb for walking is peripateo, the usual word for the conduct of a life. The Spirit and the footsteps are paired, and the language is that of a shared way of life.

Verse 19 uses oikodome, building up, and the verb of speaking is lalein, which for Paul often means speaking as one commissioned. He says he speaks 'before God in Christ,' katenanti theou en Christo, a phrase he also uses in 2:17. The courtroom of the Corinthians is replaced by the court of God.

The vices of verse 20 are eight nouns: eris, strife, zelos, jealousy, thymoi, outbursts of anger, eritheiai, rivalries or selfish ambition, katalaliai, slanders, psithyrismoi, whispers, physioseis, puffed up arrogance, and akatastasiai, disorders or tumults. The last word is the same one used of the instability of unsettled things, and it names the chaos that results from the first seven. And in verse 21 Paul says he will 'grieve,' penthesō, to mourn, the verb he used in 1 Corinthians 5:2 when he rebuked them for not mourning over sin. The three sins are akatharsia, uncleanness, porneia, sexual immorality, and aselgeia, unrestrained indecency. The same word 'humble,' tapeinoo, in verse 21 is the verb he used in 11:7 of himself: he humbled himself to lift them up, and he fears God will humble him before them.

typology.type: The shepherd who seeks the sheep, Ezekiel 34
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel condemns the shepherds who fed themselves and did not seek the lost, and promises that God Himself will search for His sheep and set one shepherd over them. Paul stands on the side of the true shepherd: he seeks them and not their possessions, and spends himself for their souls. The fulfilment in Christ is exact, for He says, 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11, and the hired hand runs away. The pattern falls short in that Paul is an under shepherd who can only point to the Shepherd, and his giving of himself cannot save.

typology.type: The prophet who grieves over Israel's sin, Jeremiah 9:1
typology.fulfillment: The prophets mourned for a people who would not turn, and Jeremiah wished that his eyes were a fountain of tears for the slain of his people. Paul's fear of grieving over those who have not repented belongs to the same line of weeping messengers. The fulfilment in Christ is that He wept over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41, and entered the city knowing it would reject Him. The type falls short in that the prophets could only mourn, but Christ bore the penalty of the sin they mourned.

typology.type: The apostle poured out like an offering, Philippians 2:17 and the sacrifices
typology.fulfillment: Paul's willingness to spend and be spent uses the language of sacrificial giving: elsewhere he says he is poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of their faith. The correspondence is with the Old Testament offerings, where something precious is given up for the sake of fellowship with God. The escalation in Christ is that He gave Himself as the offering, Ephesians 5:2, once for all. Paul's spending is a response to that and a participation in it, not an addition to it. The type falls short in that Paul's pouring out only serves the church, while Christ's saves it.

typology.type: The parent who saves for the children, Genesis 18:19 and the household of faith
typology.fulfillment: From Abraham on, God's people are told to teach their children His way, and the order of giving runs from the parent to the child. Paul applies the same order to himself and the church. It is a picture of fatherhood in the family of God. The fulfilment in Christ is that the Father gave His own Son for His children, Romans 8:32, and the heir of all things became a servant for the sake of the family. The type falls short in that human parents save for their children's future, but only the Father could give His Son to make the children His.

study.christ:
This passage leads to Christ by showing the shape of His love in the life of His servant. Paul says he seeks 'not your possessions, but you' and will 'gladly spend my money and myself' for their souls. That is how Christ loves. He did not come for what we could give, because we had nothing, but for us. 'Though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that through His poverty you might become rich,' says 2 Corinthians 8:9, a verse from the same letter. And Ephesians 5:2 says Christ gave Himself up for us as a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. Paul's spending is a small echo of that spending.

It leads to Christ by the figure of the shepherd. The false shepherds of Ezekiel 34 feed on the flock; the Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. When the hired hand sees the wolf he runs away, John 10:12, but Paul says he will stay and will spend himself, and he sends Titus and the brother as helpers and not as extractors. He does it as an apostle of the Christ who said 'whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all,' Mark 10:44, and whose own greatness was the gift of Himself.

It leads to Christ in the question of authority. The 'marks of an apostle' were done among them, but Paul does not rest on them; he rests on Christ. He speaks 'before God in Christ,' and all of his pastoral work is aimed at building up the body of which Christ is head. The apostle's aim is not to bind them to himself. In 1 Corinthians 4:15 he says he became their father through the gospel, but he has always pointed them away from himself to the Lord, and the 'one husband' of 11:2 is Christ, not Paul.

It leads to Christ in the grief over sin. Paul fears he will mourn over those who have not repented. The Lord Jesus wept over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41, longing to gather its children as a hen gathers her chicks, Luke 13:34. The pastoral grief of the apostle is the grief of the Lord in miniature, and it shows that holiness is not a mere rule but the condition of fellowship with the One who loves us.

And it leads to Christ by the promise of what He does with sin. The list of vices in verses 20 and 21 is what Christ came to deal with. He is the one who bears sin and who sends the Spirit to change hearts, so that the church need not remain in those works of the flesh. The call to repent is therefore a call to return to a Saviour who has already made the way.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Paul is not Christ, and his spending does not atone. What the passage gives is a portrait of a servant shaped by the Master, and a standard for every minister: to seek the people and not their things, and to love them to the point of being used up for their good.
study.god:
The God of this passage is the one before whom Paul speaks. 'We speak before God in Christ,' he says in verse 19. The court that matters is not the Corinthian one but the divine one, and every claim Paul makes is made under His eye. This shows a God who sees what ministers do and why they do it, who knows whether the money has been handled rightly and whether love has been real, and who will judge. For a pastor this is both a terror and a freedom: he does not need to win every argument because he is answerable to One who knows the truth.

He is a God who builds. The aim of the whole letter is to build up, oikodome, and this is what God Himself does with His people. The Lord is the builder of the house, and apostles and teachers are workers in His employ. It tells us that God's purpose for the church is growth and strength, not mere survival. Even the sharp words of the passage serve that end.

He is a God who cares about holiness. The vices of verse 20 and the sins of verse 21 are not only social inconveniences; they are things that grieve Paul and that God will deal with. The God of this passage is not indifferent to how His people live. His purpose is a church that is not only forgiven but changed, and He does not leave unrepentant sin unaddressed. The apostle fears that God may humble him in front of them, and this implies that God governs the outcome of the visit and that He is the one who deals with His church's condition.

He is a God of love that gives and does not grasp. The picture of the parent who saves for the children is, at root, a picture of the Father. Paul's willingness to spend and be spent reflects the character of the one who sent His Son. In Romans 8:32 the God who did not spare His own Son will also graciously give us all things. The giving of God is the pattern of the minister's giving, and it is also the ground of the church's confidence.

He is patient. Paul has been to Corinth twice and is writing before his third visit. The warning is given in advance so that there is time to repent. God does not hurry to judge; He sends word ahead, by messengers and letters, so that the church can change. This matches 2 Peter 3:9, where the Lord is patient, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.

For worship, the passage invites a church to take its own condition seriously and to receive correction as a sign of love. A God who warns is a God who cares. It also teaches ministers to be people who can say, before Him, that they seek the people and not their possessions.

crossReferences.note: Paul says that in Christ Jesus he became the Corinthians' father through the gospel. It is the root of the parent language in 2 Corinthians 12:14 and 15, and shows that his claim to a father's love is not a rhetorical device but the way he has always understood his relation to the church.

Paul was gentle like a nursing mother, delighted to share his own life, and worked night and day so as not to burden anyone. It is an earlier and warmer statement of the same attitude, and shows that his refusal of support at Corinth followed a consistent practice.

Paul tells the Ephesian elders that he coveted no one's silver or gold, that his own hands supplied his needs, and that it is more blessed to give than to receive. It matches the stance of 2 Corinthians 12:14 and shows that his refusal of money was part of a pattern across his ministry.

Paul is glad to be poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of the Philippians' faith. It uses a sacrificial image for the same attitude as 2 Corinthians 12:15, and shows how fully he gives himself for those he serves.

The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep, while the hired hand abandons them. This is the standard Paul's love is measured against. He does not seek what the flock can give but gives himself, as a servant of the Shepherd who gave Himself first.

The works of the flesh include strife, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish ambition, dissension and factions. The list is close to the vices Paul fears in 2 Corinthians 12:20, and shows that the sins he names are the standard marks of life in the flesh, which the Spirit is meant to replace.

Paul had earlier told the Corinthians that jealousy and dissension showed they were still worldly. The same two problems reappear in 2 Corinthians 12:20, which suggests the first letter did not fully succeed and explains the weight Paul now puts on repentance.

Paul takes care to avoid criticism in the handling of the collection, aiming to do what is right in the eyes of the Lord and of men. It is the background to the questions of 12:17 and 18 about Titus and the brother, and shows that Paul's financial dealings were open and accountable.

Paul says this is the third time he is coming and that he already warned those who sinned earlier. It continues the warning of 12:20 and 21 into the next chapter, and fixes the number of visits that stands behind 12:14.

The gifts of Christ to the church are given to build up the body until it reaches maturity. It states the goal that Paul names in 2 Corinthians 12:19, and shows that building up is the purpose of every ministry in the church, including the hard words of rebuke.

Jesus wept over Jerusalem as He approached it. Paul's fear of grieving over the unrepentant in 2 Corinthians 12:21 belongs with the Lord's own sorrow over a people who would not turn, and shows that pastoral grief is a share in Christ's.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a creator who gives, and a people made to image Him. The fall turns the human heart toward getting, and the history of Israel is full of leaders who feed on the flock. The prophets denounce them, and God promises to shepherd His people Himself, Ezekiel 34. This passage sits within that long story. Paul's refusal to seek possessions, and his love that spends and is spent, put him on the side of the true shepherd and against the false.

The story then moves to the Son, who is the Good Shepherd and who loved us and gave Himself for us. All the apostolic ministry is derived from His. Paul, at the end of a hard letter, says he seeks not your things, but you, and he is echoing what Christ has done. The relationship of giving that runs from parent to child is, in the end, the Father's giving of His Son.

The passage also continues the story of the church as the people being built up. God's purpose, from the call of Abraham, was to have a people for Himself, and the New Testament speaks of them as a temple, a body and a bride. The apostle's task is to build, and the vices he names are the things that pull the building down. Strife, jealousy and impurity are the fruit of the old Adam, and the call to repentance is the call to live in the new humanity that Christ has begun.

The passage shows that the church lives between visits, between the promise and the coming of the Lord. Paul fears what he may find when he comes, and he writes so that they may be ready. The church of every age lives in the same tension, aware that the Lord will come and that He cares how His people live. The warning is a form of love, because it is given before the day.

And the story ends where these tensions are resolved. In the new creation, there is no jealousy or strife, no impurity, no grief over those who have not repented, and the church is a bride presented without blemish, Ephesians 5:27 and Revelation 21:2. The one who was spent for them will see the fruit of his labour, and the Shepherd will wipe every tear from their eyes, Revelation 7:17. Until then, the call of the passage is to love as the apostle loved, to repent where repentance is needed, and to build one another up.

quiz.q: What does Paul point to as the marks of a true apostle?

options.text: Signs, wonders, and miracles done among them with great perseverance.
options.note: Verse 12 names these as the marks worked among the Corinthians.

options.text: His impressive speaking ability and personal charm.
options.note: Paul actually declined to compete on eloquence and outward impressiveness.

options.text: The large sums of money he collected from them.
options.note: Paul refused their support rather than gathering money for himself.

options.text: The letters of recommendation he carried.
options.note: The marks Paul cites are the works done among them and his endurance, not letters.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say he will not be a burden to the Corinthians?

options.text: Because he seeks them, not their possessions, spending himself like a parent for children.
options.note: Verses 14 and 15 give the parent image and his motive.

options.text: Because he had more than enough money of his own.
options.note: His refusal was about love and integrity, not personal wealth.

options.text: Because he thought they were too poor to help.
options.note: The reason is his self-giving love, not an assessment of their poverty.

options.text: Because an apostle is never allowed to receive support.
options.note: Paul elsewhere affirms support is legitimate; here he waives it out of love.

quiz.q: What does Paul say is the purpose of everything he writes?

options.text: To build them up, speaking before God in Christ, not to defend himself.
options.note: Verse 19 states the aim of edification.

options.text: To win the argument against the false apostles.
options.note: His concern is their growth, not merely defeating opponents.

options.text: To clear his own name at any cost.
options.note: He explicitly says it is not self-defense but their building up.

options.text: To make them feel guilty enough to obey.
options.note: The goal is edification in love, not manipulation through guilt.

quiz.q: What does Paul fear he will find when he comes to Corinth?

options.text: Quarreling, jealousy, and many who have not repented of impurity and immorality.
options.note: Verses 20 and 21 list the sins and the unrepentance he dreads.

options.text: A church that has become too wealthy and comfortable.
options.note: His fear is moral and relational sin, not prosperity.

options.text: That they will have forgotten his teaching entirely.
options.note: The specific fear is unrepented sin and disorder, not mere forgetfulness.

options.text: That the false apostles will physically attack him.
options.note: His grief is over the Corinthians' sin, not a threat of violence.

questions: Paul could claim real credentials yet called himself nothing. How do you hold together honest confidence in what God has done through you and genuine humility before Him?
Paul sought the Corinthians themselves, not their possessions. In your relationships and ministry, are you seeking people or what you can get from them?
He was willing to spend and be spent even if loved less in return. Where is God calling you to a love that keeps giving without guarantee of return?
Paul insists his hard words are meant to build up, not tear down. How do you receive correction, and how do you give it, so that it builds rather than destroys?
Paul grieved over unrepented sin among people he loved. Is there sin you have been leaving unrepented, and what would it mean to turn from it before God today?

translationNotes.note: The phrase those super-apostles is Paul's irony for the intruding false teachers; the BSB keeps the term in quotation marks.
The BSB footnote notes a more literal reading, did we not walk in the same Spirit, not in the same footsteps; the sense is that Paul and Titus acted with the same integrity toward the Corinthians.
